quiz.p: Meena sorts animals by 'can fly'. Ravi sorts the same animals by 'has hair'. Who is right?
opts: Both of them, because each rule is clear
quiz.why: Both rules are clear and anyone can check them. There are many right ways to sort. Picking only one usually comes from thinking each animal has just one true group.

quiz.p: Which is the best sorting question?
quiz.why: Anyone can check for a backbone and get the same answer. The others depend on who you ask.

quiz.p: A farmer's tomato plants died of a soil sickness. Which crop should the farmer avoid planting in that soil next?
quiz.why: Brinjal is in the tomato family, and relatives often get the same diseases. Farmers sort crops by family for this reason.

quiz.p: Which features show that tomato, brinjal and chilli are relatives?
opts: A green cap and small, flat, round seeds
They are all sold in markets
quiz.why: The green calyx and the small, flat, round seeds are shared features. Colour differs, and only the chilli is spicy.

quiz.p: Which herb has a square stem, like tulsi?
quiz.why: Mint and tulsi are in the mint family, and most of the family have square stems. Coriander and curry leaf have round stems.
People have hair, and mothers make milk for their babies. That makes people mammals. We are also primates.

quiz.p: Which of these is the biggest group?
quiz.why: Animals is the biggest. Backbone animals are inside it, mammals inside those, and primates inside the mammals.

opts: They inherited them from the same ancestors
They live in the same place
quiz.why: Living things get features from their parents, who got them from theirs. So relatives share features from shared ancestors.

quiz.p: A crow, a bat and a butterfly all have wings. Are they close relatives?
opts: Yes, because they all have wings
No, their wings are built differently and grew separately
quiz.why: Wings help each of them travel through the air, but the crow's wing has feathers, the bat's is skin on long fingers, and the butterfly's has no bones. Looks can mislead.
Mushrooms are fungi, a kingdom of their own. They make spores, not seeds, and take food from around them.

quiz.p: Carl Woese found a new big group of tiny living things in 1977. What are they called?
quiz.why: Woese and George Fox found the archaea by comparing a molecule every cell has. Fungi are a different group: mushrooms, moulds and yeast.

quiz.p: Have scientists always used the same biggest groups of life?
opts: No, they have changed them as they found new clues
quiz.why: Two kingdoms in 1735, five in 1969, three domains in 1990, and the argument goes on.

quiz.p: Lakshmi sorts her family by height, then by writing hand. The groups change. Why?
quiz.why: The people stayed the same. Each rule asks a different question, so the groups are different.

items.p: Meena sorts a crow, a pigeon and a bat into 'can fly'. Which rule would put the bat in a different group from the birds?
items.why: A bat has hair, and the crow and pigeon have feathers. The other rules put all three together.
items.art: A crow, a pigeon and a bat flying past a city building.

items.p: Which of these is a good sorting question that anyone can check?
opts: Does this one have six legs?
items.why: Anyone can count legs and get the same answer. Cute, favourite and good change from person to person.

items.p: There is only one right way to sort living things.
items.why: False. There are many right ways. Each sort is right for some job, such as cooking, farming or finding relatives.

items.p: A bat can belong to the 'can fly' group and the 'has hair' group at the same time.
items.why: True. A living thing belongs to many groups at once. Each group comes from a different question.

items.p: Sort these by the green cap at the top. Which have a green cap?
items.why: Tomato, brinjal, chilli and capsicum are in the tomato family, and they all keep a green calyx. Cucumber and pumpkin are in the gourd family.

items.p: Arjun cuts open a tomato, a brinjal and a cucumber. Which one has seeds that look different from the others?
items.why: Tomato and brinjal seeds are small, flat and round. Cucumber seeds are longer and oval, with a pointed end.

items.p: The green star on top of a tomato is called the ____.
items.why: The calyx is the ring of small green leaves that once held the flower.

items.p: Which feature do tulsi and mint share?
items.why: Tulsi and mint both have square stems, leaves in pairs and a strong smell. They are in the mint family.

items.p: People are animals.
items.why: True. People breathe, eat, grow and move, have backbones and hair, and mothers make milk for babies. People are mammals and primates.

items.p: Put these groups in order, from the biggest group to the smallest: mammal, living thing, primate, animal, backbone animal.
items.why: Each group sits inside the one before. Every primate is a mammal, every mammal has a backbone, every backbone animal is an animal, and every animal is a living thing.

items.p: A crow has a backbone and feathers. Which group are they NOT in?
items.why: A crow is a bird. Crows have feathers, not hair, so they are not mammals.

items.p: Match each food to its plant family.
items.why: Rice is a grass, moong grows in pods, brinjal keeps a green cap like the tomato, and pumpkin grows on a vine like the cucumber.

items.p: A mushroom is a kind of plant.
items.why: False. A mushroom is a fungus. They have no green leaves, cannot make food from sunlight, and make spores, not seeds.

items.p: Why do a tiger and a house cat look alike?
opts: They live in the same places
They came from the same cat ancestors
items.why: Tigers and house cats are relatives. They inherited whiskers, claws they can pull in and rough tongues from the same long-ago ancestors.

items.p: Draw two overlapping circles. Label one 'can fly' and one 'has hair'. Put a crow, a cat and a bat in the right places.
items.a: Crow in 'can fly' only, cat in 'has hair' only, bat in the middle.
items.why: The bat can fly and has hair, so they go where the circles overlap. This drawing is called a Venn diagram.

items.p: A living thing from long ago that later living things came from is called an ____.
items.why: Your grandmother's grandmother is one of your ancestors. All living things share very old ancestors.

items.p: Kavya's tomato plants died of a soil sickness. Which plant should she NOT plant in the same soil next?
items.why: Brinjal is in the tomato family, so the same sickness can attack it. The others are from different families.

items.p: A crow, a bat and a butterfly all have wings. What does this show?
opts: Different families can solve the same problem in a similar way
items.why: Their wings are built differently: feathers on an arm, skin on long fingers, and a thin sheet with no bones. Each grew separately.

items.p: Coriander has a strong smell, so it must be in the mint family.
items.why: False. Coriander smells strong, but it has a round stem and leaves that come one at a time. One clue alone can mislead.

items.p: A dolphin lives in the sea and has fins. Why is a dolphin a mammal, not a fish?
opts: They breathe air and feed their babies milk
items.why: Mammals breathe air with lungs and feed their babies milk. Dolphins do both. Fish breathe with gills.

items.p: Which of these is in the grass family?
items.why: Sugarcane is a giant grass. Their leaves are long and narrow, with veins running side by side, like rice and wheat leaves.

items.p: A mushroom left a print of fine powder on paper overnight. What was the powder made of?
items.why: Mushrooms make spores, each one a single cell. Millions together make the print.

items.p: Fungi are more closely related to ____ than to plants.
items.why: DNA comparisons show that fungi and animals share more recent ancestors than either shares with plants.

items.p: Lions and tigers have had cubs together in zoos.
items.why: True. The cubs are called ligers. Lions and tigers do not mate in the wild, so most scientists count them as two species.

items.p: Farhan writes a key. His first question is 'Is the leaf made of many small leaflets?' Which leaf goes on the 'yes' side?
items.why: A curry leaf is made of many small leaflets on one stalk. The others are single leaves.

items.p: Sort these animals: does each one have a backbone?
items.why: Crows, fish and frogs have backbones. Ants, earthworms and snails do not.

items.p: Which question puts all of these together: a neem tree, an ant and you?
items.why: All three are living things. The other questions split them.

items.p: Write two different rules that would put a cow and a crow in the same group.
items.a: For example: 'has a backbone', 'is an animal', 'has two eyes', 'can be seen in Indian streets'.
items.why: Any true rule that both answer yes to is correct. This shows that many rules can make the same group.

items.p: A potato is in the tomato family.
items.why: True. A potato plant has flowers and small green fruits like tiny tomatoes. The potato we eat is an underground stem.

items.p: Which of these is a primate?
items.why: A bonnet macaque has gripping hands, flat nails and eyes that face forward. Monkeys, apes and people are primates.

items.p: A farmer and a cook sort the same vegetables differently. Give one reason each might sort them.
items.a: The farmer sorts by family because relatives share pests and diseases. The cook sorts by cooking time or by dish.
items.why: Each sort is right for its own job.

items.p: Lakshmi sorts 4 friends by height and then by birth month. Ravi was with her in the height sort but not in the birth month sort. Did Ravi change?
items.why: Ravi stayed the same. Each question makes its own groups.

items.p: In the vegetable test, the chilli moved from the cucumber's group to the tomato's group. Explain why, using the words 'relatives' and 'features'.
items.a: Colour put the chilli with the cucumber. But the chilli shares a green cap and small, flat, round seeds with the tomato. These features were inherited from shared ancestors, so the chilli and the tomato are relatives.
items.why: Shared inherited features are clues to who is related.

items.p: Carl Woese compared one molecule in many tiny living things. What did he find?
opts: All tiny living things are the same
Some 'bacteria' were as different from bacteria as bacteria are from us
items.why: Woese and George Fox found the archaea in 1977. They look like bacteria but are very different inside.

items.p: Scientists have used the same big groups of life since 1735.
items.why: False. Linnaeus used two kingdoms. Whittaker proposed five in 1969. Woese proposed three domains in 1990. Scientists still argue about them.

items.p: Why do scientists trust a family sort more when the bodies and the DNA give the same answer?
opts: Because two kinds of evidence agree
items.why: When two separate kinds of clues point to the same family tree, it is very unlikely to be a coincidence.

items.p: Is 'has wings' a good rule for finding relatives? Give a reason.
items.a: No. Crows, bats and butterflies have wings, but they are in different families. Their wings are built differently and grew separately.
items.why: Features that do the same job can grow separately in different families.

items.p: Your hand and a bat's wing have the same set of bones. What might this tell us?
items.a: People and bats are relatives. Both are mammals, and both inherited the same arm and hand bones from shared ancestors.
items.why: The same bones used for different jobs are a strong clue to shared ancestors.

items.p: Horses and donkeys can have mules, but mules almost never have young. What do most scientists say?
opts: Horses and donkeys are one species
Horses and donkeys are two species
Mules are a third species of horse
Nobody knows what a mule is
items.why: Members of one species can usually have young that also have young. Mules almost never do, so horses and donkeys count as two species.

items.p: Some people once sorted people into groups to say some groups were better. What does science say?
items.a: A sort only shows how people answered one question, such as height. All people are one species, and any two people are almost the same in their DNA. No sort makes anyone better.
items.why: Sorting is a tool for questions, not a ranking of worth.

items.p: Archaea that make methane gas live in which of these places?
items.why: Methane-making archaea live in rice field mud, swamps and the stomachs of cows.

items.p: Kavya kept her colour sort for salads and used the family sort for the garden. Explain why both sorts are right.
items.a: The colour sort helps make a colourful salad. The family sort helps keep the garden healthy, because relatives get the same diseases. Each sort is right for its own job.
items.why: Which sort is best depends on the question you need answered.

items.p: Why does a key use yes-or-no questions about things you can see?
opts: So everyone reaches the same answer
items.why: If everyone can check the answer by looking, everyone who uses the key reaches the same name.

items.p: Make up a yes-or-no question that splits these four into two pairs: tulsi, mint, coriander, curry leaf.
items.a: 'Is the stem square?' Tulsi and mint: yes. Coriander and curry leaf: no.
items.why: The square stem is a family clue for the mint family.

items.p: All living things sense the world around them and respond.
items.why: True. A crow notices a cat, a plant senses light, and a bacterium senses sugar. Each responds in their own way.

items.p: A mushroom is closer to you than to a tulsi plant. Name one way you and a mushroom are alike that a tulsi plant is not.
items.a: Neither of us can make food from sunlight. We both get food from other living things.
items.why: Plants make their own food. Fungi and animals take food from around them.

items.p: Draw a family tree with four kitchen plant families. Put two foods on each branch.
items.a: Grass: rice, wheat. Bean: moong, chana. Tomato: tomato, chilli. Gourd: cucumber, pumpkin.
items.why: Each branch is a family of relatives, and all branches join one trunk.

applications: Farmers change crop families from season to season, so soil diseases and pests that attack one family die out.
Doctors sort snakes by their bites, so the right medicine, called antivenom, is given after a snakebite.
Seed banks and botanical gardens sort seeds and plants by family, so scientists can find relatives of crops that resist disease.
Plant breeders cross a crop with their wild relatives to give them new features, such as resistance to drought.
Doctors sort bacteria into kinds, to choose the medicine that works against each one.
Museums sort their collections of animals and plants so that any specimen can be found again.
Libraries, shops and kitchens use the same idea: groups inside groups make things quick to find.
Bird watchers and apps like iNaturalist use keys and families to name what people photograph.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of living things are there on Earth?
open_questions.why_open: About two million have names. One well-known estimate from 2011 says there may be about 8.7 million kinds of plants, animals and fungi, and there may be far more kinds of bacteria and archaea. Nobody knows.

open_questions.q: Are there two domains of life, or three?
open_questions.why_open: Some newer studies suggest that cells with a nucleus grew out of the archaea. Scientists are still collecting evidence.

open_questions.q: What did the very first living thing look like?
open_questions.why_open: It lived over 3.5 billion years ago and left no clear fossil. Scientists have ideas but no agreed answer.

open_questions.q: Where exactly does one species end and the next begin?
open_questions.why_open: Living things change slowly over many generations, and there is no single test for a species that works for all life.

open_questions.q: How do the bodies of relatives stay so alike while each family changes?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists understand a lot about how genes build bodies, but much about how features are kept or changed is still being worked out.

maths.problem: In the vegetable test, Kavya looked at 5 seeds from each of 5 vegetables. How many seeds did she look at altogether?
maths.explain: There were 5 vegetables, with 5 seeds each. 5 groups of 5 is 25. You can count in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.
maths.context: This is about the vegetable family test. You pick out 5 seeds from each vegetable to compare their shapes.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal groups tells you quickly how many seeds you need to lay out and look at.

maths.problem: Arjun has 12 living-thing cards. 7 can fly and 6 have hair. Only the bat card is in both groups. How many cards are in neither group?
maths.explain: 7 can fly and 6 have hair, which makes 13. But the bat was counted twice, so there are 13 - 1 = 12 different cards in the circles. All 12 cards are in at least one group, so 12 - 12 = 0 are in neither.
maths.context: This is about a Venn diagram, two overlapping circles. One circle is 'can fly' and one is 'has hair'. The bat goes in the middle, because they are in both.
maths.show: Two overlapping circles labelled 'can fly' and 'has hair', with a bat in the middle part.
maths.why_maths: A Venn diagram stops you counting a living thing twice when they belong to two groups.

maths.problem: In the people table, 6 people were measured. 4 were taller than 120 cm. 5 wrote with their right hand. What is the smallest number of people who could be both taller than 120 cm and right-handed?
maths.explain: There are 6 people. 4 are tall and 5 are right-handed, which makes 9. 9 is 3 more than 6. So at least 3 people must be in both groups.
maths.context: This is about the people table, where you measure everyone at home and note which hand they write with.
maths.why_maths: Reasoning with the numbers tells you something about the groups even before you look at the names.

maths.problem: Kavya has 4 grow bags. Each season, the tomato family moves one bag along. In season 1 it is in bag 1. Which bag is it in for season 4?
maths.explain: Season 1: bag 1. Season 2: bag 2. Season 3: bag 3. Season 4: bag 4. In season 5 it would go back to bag 1, like a circle.
maths.context: This is about the terrace garden challenge, where no bag grows the same plant family twice in a row.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the repeating pattern lets you plan many seasons ahead without writing each one.

maths.problem: Each round of Make a Group, Meena finds 3 true rules and Ravi finds 2. After 6 rounds, how many more rules has Meena found than Ravi?
maths.explain: Meena finds 1 more rule than Ravi each round. Over 6 rounds that is 6 × 1 = 6 more. Check: Meena 3 × 6 = 18, Ravi 2 × 6 = 12, and 18 - 12 = 6.
maths.context: This is about the card game Make a Group, where you find rules that put two living things together and leave one out.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the difference each round is quicker than adding up both totals.

roots.context: We have been sorting living things in many ways, and finding which ones are relatives. Now we ask what sorting tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Sorted by colour, the green chilli went with the cucumber. Sorted by caps and seeds, it went with the tomato and the brinjal. Those three plants share these features because they came from the same ancestor plants. So a living thing's body carries clues to their family, and careful sorting can find them.
deep_truth.habit: We think every sort of living things is a choice we make, or that things which look alike must belong together. Many sorts are useful choices. But which living things are relatives was settled long ago, by who came from whom, and their bodies still show it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the vegetable test, the colour sort and the cap-and-seed sort made different groups. The cap and the seeds put the chilli with the tomato and the brinjal. Botanists, comparing flowers and DNA, put these three in one family too.

three.who_am_i: You are a living thing, an animal, a mammal and a primate, all at once. Your body carries the clues: a backbone, hair, gripping hands.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing came from parents, and they came from theirs. So all of life is one family tree.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of relatives. A neem tree, a crow, a mushroom and you share ancestors, very long ago.

roots.thread: Long ago there were only single cells. Over billions of years, their young changed a little in each generation, and the branches split again and again. Today there are millions of kinds of living things, from bacteria to banyan trees. When we sort by shared features, we trace those branches back towards where they join. One beginning became many kinds, and each kind still carries clues to where it came from.

science.text: All living things alive today share ancestors. Their DNA, the instructions in every cell, is written in the same chemical code.
How many domains of life there are, two or three, is still being argued.
Nobody knows how many kinds of living things there are. One estimate says about 8.7 million kinds of plants, animals and fungi.

other_view.view: Being relatives is a fact about history, not a lesson about kindness. A tiger and a deer are relatives, and the tiger still hunts the deer. Whether we should treat all life as family is a question for people to decide, not something the family tree tells us.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed. Changes made: the vegetable test uses only vegetables most Indian kitchens have, with a pumpkin or bottle gourd slice if capsicum is missing, and they are cooked afterwards. A grown-up does all the cutting, and the chilli is cut last because its juice burns the eyes. The seeds are looked at five at a time on white paper, so the difference between the small round tomato-family seeds and the oval gourd seeds is easy to see. A tender cucumber still shows its soft white oval seeds. The square stem test is done with eyes closed, so the child judges by feel. Coriander and curry leaves smell strong but have round stems, which is a good lesson that one clue can mislead. Closed button mushrooms often give no spore print, so the step asks for open caps and gives what to do if nothing appears. The people table works with 3 people or with relatives on a video call. Both games work for one child alone. The spine fits about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: For most of the 1900s, scientists sorted every living thing into two groups. Some had cells with a nucleus, a small packet that holds the cell's DNA. Animals, plants and fungi were in this group. The rest had no nucleus, and they were all called bacteria. Carl Woese, an American scientist, wanted a better clue to who is related to whom. Every cell has a molecule called ribosomal RNA, which they use to build proteins. Woese compared this molecule in many tiny living things. In 1977, he and George Fox found that some 'bacteria' that make methane gas were as different from other bacteria as bacteria are from us. They called them archaebacteria. Later Woese renamed them archaea, and in 1990 he proposed three domains of life. Many biologists did not accept it at first. The famous biologist Ernst Mayr was still arguing against it in 1998. But studies of many more archaea agreed with Woese. Today they live in textbooks, and in the mud of rice fields and in our own guts.
how_we_found_out.who: Carl Woese, an American microbiologist, with George Fox, and later Otto Kandler and Mark Wheelis
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That every living thing without a nucleus is a kind of bacteria. By comparing ribosomal RNA, Woese and Fox showed that archaea are as different from bacteria as bacteria are from animals and plants.
